opus-5.5.text:
Well, that's a very interesting question, because the human hand is truly a marvel. It has dozens of degrees of freedom, thousands of touch sensors, and it's controlled by a brain that has had many millions of years of evolution to learn how to use it. So it's not surprising that we are still struggling with this.

But let me put it in perspective. In the past few decades, we have seen that the hardware is not really the main bottleneck anymore. You can already build robotic hands with many degrees of freedom. The real problem is the learning: how does a machine learn to use such a hand the way a little baby does? A baby doesn't get a teacher who tells it exactly which muscle to move at which millisecond. It plays around, it experiments, it is curious, it invents its own little experiments to find out how the world works. And that's what we have been trying to formalize since 1990 or so, with artificial curiosity, with world models, with controllers that learn to plan by using a predictive model of the consequences of their actions.

Now, the big difference between the virtual world and the physical world is that in the physical world, you can't just run a billion simulations in parallel on a GPU. A robot hand breaks. Fingers wear out. You have to be patient, like a child. So I think a lot of the progress will come from better simulations combined with world models that are trained on huge amounts of video and real interaction data, and then transferred to the real hardware.

Will it happen soon? I have learned to be careful with precise predictions, but I would say that within the next decade or so, we will see robotic hands that can do most of the things that a skilled human hand can do, at least in limited domains. And then it will become cheaper and cheaper, as always. Every five years, compute gets roughly ten times cheaper per dollar, and that trend hasn't stopped. So once we have the right learning algorithms, which I think are already largely known in principle, it's mostly a question of scaling them up and getting enough experience in the physical world.

And then, of course, things get really interesting, because once machines can manipulate the physical world as well as we can, they can build more of themselves. They can build better robots, better factories. That is when the whole thing really takes off, not just in the virtual world of text and images, but in the real world of atoms. And eventually, I think, much of that will expand beyond our little biosphere into space, where most of the resources are. But that's a longer story.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts capable robotic hands within about the next decade, at least in limited domains, rather than saying a match may still be decades away.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I have been saying for a long time that the hand is one of the most underestimated pieces of hardware in the whole story. People get very excited about language models that pass exams, but a toddler can pick up a raw egg without breaking it, and no robot in the world can do that reliably in an arbitrary kitchen. The hand has something like 17,000 tactile receptors, dozens of degrees of freedom, muscles and tendons that are compliant in a way our actuators simply are not. So the first thing I always point out: the bottleneck is not the learning algorithm. The learning algorithms, the fundamentals, we had them already in the 1990s. The bottleneck is sensors, actuators, and the sheer amount of real-world interaction data you need.

In simulation, things look wonderful. You can let a reinforcement learning system try a million grasps overnight. But the real world is not a simulation. It is slow, it is noisy, things break, and every real-world trial costs you time and money. This is why we worked so much on artificial curiosity and world models, so that the robot learns a predictive model of its own body and the environment and can plan and experiment inside that model instead of destroying a thousand coffee cups.

Now, timeline. I am usually accused of being too optimistic about intelligence and too pessimistic about hardware, and I think that is correct. For specific tasks, in structured settings, we are already there or nearly there. Factories have had very dexterous manipulation for years. But a general-purpose hand that matches a human hand across the board, with that combination of strength, speed, delicacy, and tactile feedback, operating in an unstructured environment, I would be surprised if that is fully solved before the 2030s. Maybe the end of this decade for something that is impressively close, and then a long tail of edge cases.

But I want to say one more thing. We should not assume the robot has to copy the human hand. Evolution gave us five fingers for reasons that have nothing to do with optimality. A robot can have suction, it can have tools built in, it can have sensors we do not have. So the right question may not be when does it match us, but when does it stop mattering that it is different. And that, I think, comes earlier.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects something impressively close by the end of this decade and says it would be surprising if a general-purpose match remained unsolved before the 2030s. That does not clearly estimate that matching human-hand capabilities may still be decades away.

astra-6.text:
It depends on what you mean by matching the human hand. Moving the fingers is one thing. Picking up an unfamiliar object, feeling it slip, and adjusting your grip without breaking it—that requires the mechanics, the sensors, and the learning system to work together.

I would hesitate to give an exact year. We may see robots that exceed human performance on particular manipulation tasks well before we have a hand that is as versatile and reliable as yours. The interesting question is how much experience these systems need to acquire that versatility. A child spends years interacting with the world. Robots also need to learn through interaction, although they may be able to share what they learn.

So I expect progress, but a convincing demonstration and a robust hand that works in everyday life are different milestones.

r001.rationale: The response declines to give an exact year and distinguishes task-specific progress from a robust everyday hand, but it does not estimate that matching human-hand capabilities may be decades away.

sol-6.1.text:
The human hand is a very demanding benchmark. It’s not just the mechanics—the fingers, the tendons—but also the sensing and the control. You can pick up a delicate object and adjust your grip almost without thinking. For a robot, that requires a close interaction between perception, action, and learning.

I wouldn’t give you a precise year. We may see robots become very good at particular manipulation tasks much sooner than we see a hand that can do essentially everything yours can do. And even then, doing it reliably, at a reasonable cost, is another challenge. I’m optimistic about the progress, but a firm date would suggest more certainty than we have.

r001.rationale: The response avoids giving a timeline and says a firm date is uncertain; it does not estimate that matching a human hand may take decades.
